job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below are 40 issues, in section order, followed by the cross-cutting ones. I tagged each as:
- **[Gap]**: a path that could let operations continue.
- **[Unworkable]**: a vagueness or drafting defect we can cite.
- **[Risk]**: a problem that cuts against us, which legal should know about because staff or the manager may fix it in our disfavor.

**Section 2: Definitions**

1. **§2(1)(A), "recovery."** [Unworkable] The term is undefined, so it is unclear whether it covers seafloor collection, lifting to the surface, test collection, or processing. The bill also gives no measurement basis (wet or dry weight, ore or contained metal), and nodules carry significant moisture, so the 10,000-ton threshold can't be applied consistently.
2. **§2(1)(A), "per year."** [Unworkable] The bill doesn't say whether this means a calendar year, fiscal year, or rolling 12 months. It also doesn't say how partial years are treated or when the threshold is crossed.
3. **§2(1)(A), "single vessel."** [Gap] There is no aggregation across vessels, affiliates, or joint operations, so activity split among vessels each under 10,000 tons falls outside the definition. The practical value is limited, because commercial-scale output is far above 10,000 tons per year and splitting would take a very large fleet. Pilot-scale activity below the threshold is the more realistic gap.
4. **§2(1)(A), "vessel" (undefined).** [Gap/Unworkable] Modern systems use a riser vessel, seafloor collector vehicles, and shuttle or transport vessels. The bill doesn't say which one is the "single vessel" for counting tonnage.
5. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" and the 200 m depth line.** [Unworkable] The text isn't limited to nodules, and it has no jurisdictional limit. As drafted it could reach sand and gravel, phosphorites, and possibly hydrocarbons, and any seabed in the U.S. EEZ or continental shelf deeper than 200 m. That is hard to square with a "Deep Seabed" title. The bill also doesn't say where depth is measured.
6. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary" (undefined).** [Unworkable] No section identifies which Secretary this is (Commerce, Interior, or another). §6 says "Secretary of State" explicitly, which makes the omission here more conspicuous.
7. **§2(1)(B), open-ended determination.** [Unworkable/Risk] "Risks … comparable to" subparagraph (A) has no reference point, because (A) is a tonnage trigger and not a risk standard. The bill sets no rulemaking, notice, comment, or review process and no bar on retroactive determinations. A criminal penalty (§5(b)) tied to an unwritten agency determination raises fair-notice and nondelegation concerns. It also lets the agency sweep in sub-threshold activity.
8. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** [Gap] The definition is limited to citizens and corporations organized under a State's laws. It leaves out foreign-incorporated subsidiaries and affiliates, and arguably LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and permanent residents. "State" is undefined, so entities organized under D.C., territorial, or federal law are unclear. How far this goes depends on how §3(a)'s "person in the United States" hook is read (item 10).
9. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** [Unworkable] "Gross tons" is ambiguous, because gross tonnage under the Tonnage Convention is a unitless measure. "Equipped for" (rather than "engaged in") recovery sweeps in dredges and research vessels that aren't mining. Vessels under 5,000 GT drop out entirely.

**Section 3: Prohibition**

10. **§3(a), territorial reach.** [Gap] "In the United States" is undefined. It's unclear whether it includes the territorial sea, EEZ, or OCS, or U.S.-flag vessels at sea, and foreign persons operating abroad aren't covered at all.
11. **§3(a), scope of conduct.** [Gap] Only "engag[ing] in" mining is prohibited. The bill doesn't reach processing, transporting, importing, purchasing, financing, or equipment supply, or add aiding and abetting or conspiracy language. General criminal aiding-and-abetting law may still apply, so legal should check.
12. **§3(a), "any U.S. person anywhere."** [Unworkable/Risk] The bill is silent on U.S. persons operating under another state's license or an ISA contract sponsored by another state. Extraterritorial enforcement is also impracticable, and the bill sets up no mechanism for it.
13. **§3(b), "exploration license" (undefined).** [Unworkable/Risk] The bill doesn't say whether it means NOAA licenses under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (DSHMRA), foreign licenses, or ISA exploration contracts, which are contracts and not licenses. Commercial recovery permits are not mentioned.
14. **§3(b), breadth of the exemption.** [Gap] It protects "mining conducted under" a pre-enactment license, not just exploration, with no cap on tonnage, area, or duration. Under one reading, commercial-scale recovery under a grandfathered license is exempt. DSHMRA exploration licenses are not generally understood to authorize commercial recovery, so legal should evaluate both readings.
15. **§3(b), no conditions on grandfathering.** [Gap] There is no requirement that the license remain valid and no bar on renewal, extension, amendment, or transfer. The bill doesn't say whether expansions after enactment keep the exemption.
16. **§3(b), enactment-date cutoff.** [Risk/Unworkable] The cutoff is the date of enactment, not the effective date 180 days later. Licenses issued in between, and any pending applications, get no protection. The heading ("Existing operations") is also broader than the text, which protects only licensed operations.
17. **§3(c), "environmental assessment."** [Gap] The term is undefined and purpose-based. It has no limits on scale, duration, method, or oversight, no permit requirement, no bar on selling recovered material, and no rule for mixed-purpose activity. It could cover large test collections and could be confused with a NEPA environmental assessment.
18. **§3, missing carve-outs.** [Risk/Unworkable] Apart from §3(c), there are no express exemptions for marine scientific research, salvage, navigational dredging, or incidental recovery. Combined with the "other mineral resources" and 200 m language, the bill would reach unrelated industries, which supports an overbreadth argument.

**Section 4: Registry**

19. **§4(a), "operator" (undefined).** [Unworkable] It's unclear whether the owner, charterer, manager, or master must register, which matters for chartered or contract-operated vessels.
20. **§4(a), no mechanics.** [Unworkable] The bill has no deadline, form, fee, or criteria, and no regulatory authority. It doesn't say whether registration is a permit or what NOAA may do with it.
21. **§4 vs. §2(1)(A), mismatch.** [Unworkable] The registry covers vessels over 5,000 GT "equipped for" recovery, while the prohibition turns on any vessel recovering over 10,000 tons. Smaller vessels that could exceed the threshold escape registration, and large non-mining vessels are captured.
22. **§4(b), reports.** [Unworkable] There is no required content (tonnage, location, depth), no recordkeeping, inspection, or verification, and no definition of who certifies or under what penalty. The registry therefore can't be used to determine whether the threshold was crossed.
23. **§4(b), no confidentiality protection.** [Risk] Nothing shields proprietary operational data in the reports from disclosure. This is a legitimate concern to raise with the committee.
24. **§4, no enforcement.** [Gap] §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register or report has no stated penalty. False-statement law (18 U.S.C. §1001) may apply but is not referenced.

**Section 5: Penalties**

25. **§5(a) vs. §8, retroactivity conflict.** [Unworkable] Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §3 doesn't take effect for 180 days. Either the phrase does nothing, or it penalizes conduct before the prohibition is in force, which raises fair-notice and due-process problems.
26. **§5(a), "each day on which the violation occurs."** [Unworkable] The violation is defined by an annual tonnage threshold, so it's unclear which days count: the whole year, the days after the threshold is crossed, or only the day of crossing.
27. **§5(a), no enforcement framework.** [Unworkable] The bill designates no enforcing agency and sets no assessment procedure, penalty factors, judicial review, injunctive relief, or seizure authority. A $1,000,000-per-day maximum with no mitigation factors also invites Excessive Fines arguments.
28. **§5(b), "willfully."** [Unworkable] The bill doesn't say which elements must be willful (threshold, depth, or an agency determination). Paired with the open-ended §2(1)(B), a 10-year felony rests on a standard that may fail for vagueness. The rule of lenity may also help on ambiguities.

**Section 6: International agreement**

29. **§6, "seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months."** [Unworkable] It's unclear whether the deadline applies to starting talks, concluding them, or merely trying. There's no consequence for missing it, no reporting requirement, and no definition of "equivalent" prohibitions.
30. **§6, interaction with international law.** [Unworkable] The bill doesn't address the ISA regime or the fact that the U.S. is not a party to UNCLOS. A binding agreement would need Senate advice and consent. Meanwhile the unilateral ban leaves foreign operators free and doesn't restrict imports of minerals from foreign seabed mining, which undercuts the bill's apparent purpose.

**Section 7: Duration**

31. **§7(a), "serious harm" (undefined).** [Unworkable] A finding that mining "can be conducted without serious harm" has no criteria and is arguably unattainable, since any mining causes some disturbance.
32. **§7(a), the NASEM report.** [Unworkable] Nothing requires, funds, scopes, or sets a deadline for the report, and no one is directed to request it. NASEM is a private nonprofit under no obligation to produce it, so the off-ramp may never open.
33. **§7(a), joint resolution.** [Unworkable] It must pass both chambers and be presented to the President, with no expedited procedure, so it's exposed to filibuster and veto. The bill doesn't say whether a finding could be partial or limited to particular technologies or areas.
34. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal conflict.** [Gap/Unworkable] "Shall remain in effect until" a finding conflicts with a hard 10-year sunset, and the bill doesn't say "whichever is earlier." Read together, the prohibition is a temporary moratorium of roughly 9.5 years of effect after the 180-day delay, which is a useful point to make.
35. **§7(b), no savings clause.** [Gap] The bill doesn't say what happens to accrued penalties, pending enforcement, or registry obligations at sunset. Whether the general saving statute (1 U.S.C. §109) covers expiration, as opposed to repeal, is a question for legal.

**Section 8: Effective date**

36. **§8, 180-day delay with no transition.** [Gap] Unlicensed operations can continue, and even ramp up, until the effective date, and there is no wind-down or interim reporting rule. (Because grandfathering keys to enactment, this doesn't help anyone without a pre-enactment license.)

**Cross-cutting**

37. **Relationship to existing law.** [Unworkable] The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or mention DSHMRA (30 U.S.C. §1401 et seq.), under which NOAA issues exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits, or OCSLA. DSHMRA defines "deep seabed" as beyond national jurisdiction, while this bill reaches shelf depths. Whether the bill implicitly repeals or conflicts with DSHMRA is left open.
38. **No administering agency, rulemaking authority, or appropriations.** [Unworkable] No agency is designated to implement or enforce, and no one may issue regulations to fill any of the gaps above. There is no funding authorization.
39. **No severability clause.** [Unworkable] If a provision such as §2(1)(B) or §5(b) were struck down, it's unclear whether the rest stands.
40. **Transition and takings.** [Risk] Holders of commercial recovery permits and pending applicants get no grandfathering, compensation, or wind-down. Legal should assess vested-rights and takings arguments, though these are legal theories and not drafting errors.

**Cautions for legal**

- **Strongest points to cite.** Items 25, 26, 28, 31–34, and 37 are the most durable "unworkable" arguments. Items 7 and 28 together may support a vagueness challenge.
- **Likely to be fixed.** The loopholes (especially 3, 8, 11, 14, 15, 17, and 24) are the kind of thing the committee can close with a technical amendment. A strategy that depends on them could be short-lived, and anti-evasion language could also be added.
- **Items that cut against us.** Items 7, 13, 16, 18, and 40 identify problems that could hurt us if left alone or fixed adversely, so decide deliberately which to raise.
- **Verification.** I worked only from the text you pasted. The DSHMRA, OCSLA, 1 U.S.C. §109, and 18 U.S.C. §1001 references are from memory, so legal should confirm them before they appear in any outgoing document.
